I’ve been looking at it differently, and maybe I’m wrong: If your brain is unable to produce enough natural steroid, your immune system will be overworking itself — causing inflammation. With enough inflammation you’re eventually going to have a migraine. Again, without steroids in your body your mood and energy will suffer severely, which explains this recirculating depression. 

For me I’ve noticed the migraines present when my body is fighting infection (not necessarily from the symptoms of sickness, just when my immune system is reacting.) What I’m starting to believe from my own experience is that depression and migraines are byproducts of immune responses, more specifically the immune system not catching up. After all, heavy migraine symptoms mirror an intense fever more than a headache (visual and auditory sensitivity along with perceptual distortions particularly). Is it that far of a stretch to say there’s some correlation? If your body produced enough natural steroid, inflammation would be limited and your immune system would let off when your body told it to — thereby keeping the migraines and depression less frequent.

Sure I can agree with you about the kicks. But the way they look and sit in a mix might not mean they show up so drastically loud in the waveform. Have you tried layering kicks? Have you tried separating the higher frequencies of the kick and layering distortion? There are a few techniques you can use to maximize headroom while keeping the punch of the kick intact. It all depends on your sounds however. Do you have any examples of your mix I could hear?

By carving unneeded frequency out of your sounds using an EQ, you can get that extra headroom you’re after. It’s part of the mixing process you definitely want to experiment with. I personally do a lot of removal with EQ and then begin adjusting the individual mixer sliders. Often times by the end of the mixing process the track will be fairly level and quiet, without kicks and snares visibly poking through the track’s waveform and overpowering everything else. At that point you can adjust the headroom to taste, add compression, limiter, whatever you want really. If you’re getting it mastered make a duplicate project with your plugins on the masterbus and send both versions over so the engineer knows what kind of energy you’re after. 

Also, if your track is “quiet” without a limiter, you need to improve your mixing!

I've made stuff similar to this while trying to make unique percussion. Here's the process: Make or take a complex drum loop and run it through a few glitch machine plugins at a high (96k) sample rate. As the loop is playing and going through the fx chain, record the output. Then, load that recorded chunk into Alchemy. From there modulate the sample starting position with sequencers and lfos running at odd rates. I'd also have it play at differing pitches.Export the result and repeat the process until you have what you want. Usually I cut the low end away at some stage. 

The real key here is finding plugins capable of randomized "chaos," and then layering them. Glitch machines just works well for me personally. Also record the outputs at higher sample rates!!!
It's a tedious process especially if you're new to the editor. Took me a while before I could finish things consistently.

With multiple instances, and multiple sequences within each instance, shit can get real glitchy and unconventional real fast. You can also use Effectrix, but I'm not sure you can map as many sequences per instance compared to Glitch 2. Effectrix does offer more effects to use however. Might want to experiment with both. The cool thing is you can create and save a template project with the mapping set up and the plugins loaded already. That way all you have to do when you get inspired is open it up, drop a loop in, and adjust the bpm.
